common_name: Sugar Lace II Snap Pea (Semi-Leafless AAS Winner)

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked, 4-6 weeks before the last frost; the compact, mostly self-supporting vines need little or no trellising compared to standard snap peas.

directions: Sugar Lace II is a semi-leafless snap pea, meaning many of its leaflets are replaced by extra curling tendrils that let neighboring plants hook together into a self-supporting mass, reducing or eliminating the need for a trellis. It was recognized as an All-America Selections winner for combining good disease tolerance, including resistance to powdery mildew, with heavy sets of sweet, crisp, stringless pods that are eaten whole. Direct sow early in cool soil and keep evenly moist through flowering and pod fill for the best flavor and texture. Harvest when pods are plump and glossy but before they lose their bright green color.

common_name: Super Sugar Snap Pea (Improved High-Yield Snap Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow as early as the soil can be worked and set a sturdy 5-6 foot trellis at planting time, since vines are tall and vigorous and set pods quickly once warm days arrive.

directions: Super Sugar Snap is an improved selection bred from the original Sugar Snap pea to offer stronger vigor, better tolerance of powdery mildew, and a few days' earlier, heavier first flush of pods. The tall vines still need a sturdy trellis or fence but reward the extra support with thick-walled, sweet, fully edible pods over a longer harvest window than the older strain. Pick every two to three days once pods are round and glossy to keep plants producing and to catch pods before the pod wall starts to toughen. Because it holds up well to warm spring weather, it is a good choice for gardeners in regions where the cool pea season is short.

planting.note: Sow directly in cool soil as early as it can be worked, and give vines a tall trellis or fence to climb, since this heirloom grows considerably taller than most modern snap peas.

directions: Amish Snap is a tall heirloom snap pea passed down through Amish and Mennonite farm families in Pennsylvania and the Midwest and preserved by seed savers rather than commercial breeding programs. Vigorous vines climb readily on a trellis and set heavy quantities of sweet, plump, stringless pods that hold their quality well in variable spring weather. Because the vines are unusually tall, plan on netting or a fence at least five to six feet high and harvest every couple of days once pods fill out to keep the plants productive. The pods are good eaten fresh off the vine, lightly steamed, or stir-fried.

common_name: Blauwschokker Pea (Purple Podded Dutch Soup Pea, Capucijner)

planting.note: Direct sow in cool soil as early as it can be worked; provide a trellis for the four to five foot vines and decide at planting whether you plan to pick pods green for fresh shelling or leave them to dry for soup peas.

directions: Blauwschokker is a centuries-old Dutch heirloom prized for its bicolor purple-and-white flowers and deep violet pods, making it as ornamental as it is useful in the vegetable garden. Pods can be picked young and shelled fresh like a standard garden pea, or left on the vine until they dry to a papery tan for storage as a marbled grey-green soup pea, traditionally used in Dutch pea soup. The vigorous climbing vines benefit from a trellis and produce over a long picking window in cool weather. This variety is a good choice for gardeners who want a dual-purpose pea that also adds color to a spring garden.

common_name: Corne de Bélier Snow Pea (Ram's Horn Pea)
scientific_name: Pisum sativum var. saccharatum 'Corne de Bélier'

planting.note: Direct sow in cool soil as early as it can be worked and provide a trellis; pick pods while still young and flat for the best flavor and texture, since this snow pea toughens quickly once peas begin to swell.

directions: Corne de Bélier, French for ram's horn, is a classic French heirloom snow pea named for its long, curved, flattened pods. The vigorous climbing vines produce attractive bicolor flowers followed by an abundant set of stringless, tender pods best harvested while young and flat for stir-fries, salads, and quick sautés. It is a long-standing favorite in French market gardens and heirloom seed collections both for its culinary use and for its ornamental flowers. Provide a trellis and pick frequently to keep pods tender and encourage continued production.

common_name: Thomas Laxton Pea (Heirloom English Main-Crop Shelling Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as the soil can be worked in early spring; the medium-height vines benefit from light staking or pea netting to keep pods off the ground and easy to pick.

directions: Thomas Laxton was introduced in England in 1898 by the Laxton Brothers breeding firm as an improved early-to-main-season shelling pea and has remained popular with seed savers ever since for its reliable yields and classic sweet English pea flavor. Vines are shorter and easier to manage than tall telephone-type peas but still produce well-filled pods over a solid harvest window. Sow early for the sweetest peas, and pick pods promptly once they fill out, since flavor declines quickly as peas mature and starch content rises. Its heirloom status and open-pollinated seed make it a good choice for gardeners who want to save their own seed year to year.

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has thoroughly warmed and all frost danger has passed; this compact, semi-bush type is well suited to gardens with a history of root-knot nematode or Fusarium wilt problems.

directions: Coronet was developed through a Southern land-grant university breeding program as a compact, semi-bush cream-type southern pea selected for resistance to root-knot nematodes and Fusarium wilt, two soil-borne problems that plague many older cowpea varieties in the Deep South. It holds its pods well above the foliage, making hand-picking easier than with sprawling types. Like other cowpeas, it thrives in hot, humid summer weather that stresses most other vegetable crops and fixes nitrogen in the soil through root nodules, benefiting whatever is planted after it. Harvest pods at the green-shell stage for fresh cream peas or allow them to dry fully on the vine for storage.
